From core to surface. Explore layers by composition, then examine the rigid shell and deformable mantle.
Plates are pieces of lithosphere. Explore their boundaries and the processes that create oceans, volcanoes and earthquakes.
A mountain has several histories: the age of its rocks, their deformation, then the building and erosion of its relief.
Each rock preserves clues to its origin. Read a cross-section, observe transformations and discover how events are dated.

About

Drawings are teaching diagrams, not reconstructions of real sites. Colours identify materials; they do not represent observed colours. Motion is greatly accelerated and arrows explain mechanisms rather than a physical simulation. Local sections exaggerate thickness and relief.

An internal layer has no single age. A rock can preserve several ages: deposition, crystallisation, metamorphism and cooling. Mountain ages depend on the event being dated.

Periods reuse the ICS 2026/06 data already in the timeline; boundaries without a stated uncertainty are not necessarily exact. Tree links concern relevant living groups without assigning their origin dates to rocks.

ICS · chronostratigraphic scale
Crust
About 5–10 km beneath oceans; 30–70 km beneath continents.
Early crust formed as Earth cooled about 4.54 billion years ago; it has been extensively reworked.
It is a compositional layer, not a whole plate. Its age varies by rock: today\'s crust does not all date from Earth\'s birth.
Upper mantle
From the Moho to about 660 km depth; magnesium- and iron-rich silicates.
Inherited from early Earth differentiation, it changes mineralogy with pressure; a transition zone lies around 410–660 km.
It is mainly solid. Hot rock can deform slowly without becoming an ocean of magma.
Lower mantle
About 660–2,900 km depth; solid and very hot under high pressure.
Minerals become denser at depth. This mineralogical boundary is not a layer deposited at a particular date.
Convection is slow deformation of solid material over long times. Heat comes partly from cooling and natural radioactivity.
Outer core
About 2,900–5,150 km depth; a liquid alloy dominated by iron.
Dense metals accumulated towards the centre during Earth\'s early differentiation.
Motion of the conducting liquid, together with Earth\'s rotation, sustains the magnetic field. Seismic waves help reveal its liquid state.
Inner core
From 5,150 km to the centre at 6,371 km; radius about 1,220 km; solid.
It grows as the liquid core crystallises during cooling. Its formation age remains debated; no single date is assigned here.
High pressure stabilises the solid despite the high temperature. Inner and outer core belong to the same metallic region.
Oceanic crust
Often about 7 km thick; basalt and gabbro.
It forms at ridges as magma cools, then moves away, cools and can be recycled by subduction.
Major ocean floors are generally younger than 200 million years. This is not an absolute limit for every preserved oceanic remnant.
Continental crust
About 30–70 km; varied composition, on average less dense than oceanic crust.
It grows and is recycled through magmatism, collisions and accretion. Some continental cores preserve rocks older than 4 billion years.
A continent combines terrains of different ages. Young sediments can cover a very ancient basement.
Mohorovičić discontinuity
Boundary between crust and mantle; variable depth.
Identified through changes in seismic-wave velocity; it is neither a rock nor a stratum.
The Moho is deeper beneath ranges with thickened crust. It mainly separates different compositions; it does not mark the bottom of plates.
Lithosphere
Crust plus rigid uppermost mantle; thickness varies from tens to hundreds of kilometres.
It cools and thickens, particularly as it ages away from ridges. It is divided into plates.
The lithosphere–asthenosphere distinction concerns mechanical behaviour, not just composition. A plate can carry both continent and ocean.
Asthenosphere
Deformable upper-mantle region beneath the lithosphere; variable boundaries.
Temperature allows slow deformation. It has neither a uniform thickness nor a single formation date everywhere.
It remains mainly solid. Plates do not float on a bath of magma; partial melting is localised.
Mid-ocean ridge
Divergent boundary; new oceanic crust forms.
Plate separation allows mantle to rise; falling pressure causes partial melting.
Magma crystallises at depth or reaches the seafloor. Rocks are younger near the axis and age as they move away.
Continental rift
Continental extension; normal faults and a down-dropped valley.
Lithosphere stretches and thins. Some rifts evolve into oceans; others stop.
The East African Rift is an active example. Blocks tilt and basins accumulate sediment; volcanism varies by region.
What moves plates
Speeds generally of the order of a few centimetres per year.
Motion is part of Earth\'s thermal and gravitational system, maintained over hundreds of millions of years.
Sinking-slab pull, ridge-related forces and mantle interactions act together. Arrows summarise this complex system.
Age of the ocean floor
Age generally increases on either side of a ridge.
Radiometric measurements and magnetic bands record progressive seafloor formation.
Cooling thickens lithosphere and increases its density. Bands are not stacked strata: they lie side by side horizontally.
Subduction
One plate sinks beneath another; lithosphere is recycled.
Cold oceanic lithosphere can become dense enough to sink into the mantle.
Fluids released by the slab promote melting in the mantle above. The sinking plate does not simply melt in its entirety.
Trench and accretionary prism
Oceanic depression and, sometimes, piles of scraped-off sediment.
Bending of the sinking plate forms a trench; some sediment can be transferred to the overriding plate.
Not every margin builds a large prism: some lose material through tectonic erosion.
Volcanic arc
A line of volcanoes above subduction.
Water and other fluids released at depth lower the melting temperature of mantle rocks.
Magma rises, may reside in the crust and can feed volcanoes. An arc can be continental, like the Andes, or an island arc.
Earthquakes and rupture
Rapid rupture after elastic deformation accumulates.
Parts of faults can remain locked while plates keep moving.
Rupture releases waves. In subduction, earthquake locations outline the slab; the diagram predicts neither date nor magnitude.
Continental collision
Crustal shortening and thickening.
After an ocean closes, two continental domains can meet and build a mountain range.
Rocks fold, thrust over one another and undergo metamorphism. Relief develops through long evolution, not an instantaneous impact.
Folds
Bent layers: anticlines and synclines.
Progressive deformation bends layers, particularly under compression.
An anticline normally has older rocks in its core; a syncline has younger rocks. Overturned folds make interpretation harder.
Crustal root
Crust is often thicker beneath a major range.
Shortening stacks rocks and thickens the crust upwards and downwards.
A root illustrates gravitational balance, not an exact upside-down mountain. Lithospheric strength distributes loads.
Transform boundary
Two plates slide past one another.
Relative movement is accommodated by strike-slip faults; San Andreas is an example.
A transform boundary neither directly creates nor consumes lithosphere. Local bends can cause compression or extension.
Hotspot
Volcanism that can occur away from plate boundaries.
A hot mantle anomaly promotes partial melting; some hotspots are associated with deep plumes.
A hotspot is not necessarily stationary. The drawn plume is a schematic interpretation; real systems are more complex.
Hawaiian chain
Islands and seamounts of successive ages.
Movement of the Pacific Plate above a volcanic source builds a chain.
Volcanoes move away from the active region, erode and subside. Their age generally increases with distance, without being a universal rule.
Major plates
Pacific, North American, South American, African, Eurasian, Antarctic; Indian and Australian domains.
Today\'s arrangement results from opening and closing oceans. It also includes smaller plates: Nazca, Cocos, Arabian, Philippine Sea…
A plate does not correspond to a continent. The India–Australia boundary is diffuse and the number of plates depends on the level of detail.
Thrust faults
One body of rock moves over another.
Compression creates reverse faults, sometimes with shallow slopes, that transport thrust sheets.
Old rocks can overlie younger rocks. The simple \'old below\' rule no longer suffices in a deformed section.
Alps
Alpine range; major Cenozoic collision, notably around 35–30 Ma in the Western Alps.
Closure of oceanic domains followed by Europe–Adria convergence stacked and exhumed rocks.
Marine limestones and much older basement rocks form today\'s peaks. An Alpine rock can be much older than the mountain relief.
Himalayas
India–Eurasia collision began roughly 60–50 Ma, depending on the criteria used.
Convergence after closure of Tethys thickened crust and built the Himalayas and Tibetan Plateau.
Deformation continues. Today\'s height reflects competition between uplift, erosion and reorganisation of rocks.
Andes
Active-margin range; Nazca subducts beneath South America.
Its history spans many phases; major stages of today\'s relief developed during the Cenozoic.
Compression and magmatism build the range. Segments differ in age and volcanism.
Normal fault
One block moves down relative to another during extension.
Stretching breaks crust into uplifted and down-dropped blocks.
Horsts and grabens produce mountains and basins. A mountain can therefore form through extension without continental collision.
Erosion and transport
Water, wind, gravity and ice reshape relief.
Weathering breaks down or transforms rocks; erosion removes and transports material.
Debris becomes sediment in basins. A range can erode while it rises: relief and motion are not the same.
Glacial imprint
U-shaped valleys, cirques, moraines and polished rocks.
Moving ice plucks and abrades bedrock; debris is deposited as it melts.
Quaternary glaciations extensively reshaped mountains. Valley carving is younger than the rocks it cuts.
Isostasy
Gravitational readjustment of lithosphere over mantle.
Adding or removing load changes the balance: crustal thickening, erosion or ice-sheet melting.
Rebound can continue long after load removal. Mantle responds slowly; the diagram amplifies this movement.
Ancient ranges
Appalachians and Variscan landscapes: legacies of Palaeozoic mountain building.
Collisions contributed to Pangaea\'s assembly, notably during the Carboniferous and Permian.
Visible relief may reflect later uplift. Ancient basement does not mean every hill has kept its shape for 300 million years.
Deposition and lithification
Particles or precipitates become sedimentary rock.
Deposits accumulate in rivers, lakes, seas or deserts; compaction and cementation consolidate them.
Thickness depends on supply and available space, not simply duration. The section is illustrative and represents no dated site.
Sandstone
Cemented sand grains; often rich in quartz.
Sand transported by water or wind settles and then consolidates.
Grain size and laminations reveal transport conditions. Sandstone can be ancient or young; its name assigns no age.
Limestone
Carbonate rock, often rich in calcite.
It may form from shell debris, biological activity or chemical precipitation.
Marine limestone now in mountains records deposition followed by deformation and uplift. The mollusc link explores shell-producing organisms.
Mudstones and shales
Very fine-grained rocks formed from consolidated mud.
Fine particles often settle in quiet water, then become compacted.
A mudstone is not necessarily a metamorphic schist. Properties depend on composition and rock history.
Fossils and ancient environments
Organism remains or traces preserved in rocks.
Burial, mineralisation and local conditions determine preservation; the record is incomplete.
Assemblages help correlate layers and reconstruct environments. The first known fossil does not precisely date a group\'s origin.
Igneous rocks
Rocks formed by solidification of magma or lava.
Partial melting produces magma that cools in the crust or at the surface.
Slow cooling favours large crystals; rapid cooling often produces small crystals or glass.
Granite
Plutonic rock, notably containing quartz and feldspars.
Magma crystallises slowly at depth; erosion can later expose it.
Crystallisation date is neither surface-exposure date nor the age of today\'s relief. Continents are not made solely of granite.
Basalt
Dark volcanic rock; common deep equivalent: gabbro.
Relatively silica-poor lava cools rapidly at the surface or on the seafloor.
Basalt is common at ridges and some hotspots. Underwater lava can form pillows.
Metamorphism
Solid-state transformation under new conditions.
Temperature, pressure and fluids alter the minerals and textures of an existing rock.
Limestone can become marble, granite can become gneiss. Metamorphism does not require total melting: melting produces magma.
Rock cycle
Several possible pathways; no compulsory order.
Weathering, deposition, burial, metamorphism, melting and crystallisation connect rock families.
A rock can be recycled repeatedly or remain stable for a long time. The diagram shows possibilities, not a loop every rock follows.
Superposition
In a non-overturned sequence, lower layers are older.
Deposits accumulate successively; most begin approximately horizontally.
This rule gives a relative order, not a numerical date. Folds, faults and thrusts require checking whether the sequence was disturbed.
Unconformity and gaps
A surface separates a discontinuous record.
A pause in deposition or erosion removes part of the history; new deposits later cover older ones.
Tilted beds beneath horizontal beds indicate an angular unconformity. A thin boundary can hide a very long missing interval.
How are rocks dated?
Relative ages from relationships; numerical ages from suitable methods.
Radioactive isotopes and their decay products can date mineral crystallisation or cooling.
An ancient grain in sediment predates deposition. Identify the measured event and its uncertainty; carbon-14 cannot date all Earth history.
Cross-cutting relationships
A structure cutting another is younger.
A fault offsets existing layers; an igneous dyke cuts older rocks.
Combine cross-cutting, superposition and dating to order events. A single section can preserve multiple episodes.
